{"id": "665c96d6-aeef-4501-839a-012da57e989c", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_FzWKXBJTHqN1h4c6gN5Emo", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Tag your Amazon EC2 resources\",\"context\":\"## Tag restrictions\\n\\nThe following basic restrictions apply to tags:\\n\\n* Maximum number of tags per resource \u2013 50\\n* For each resource, each tag key must be unique, and each tag key can have only\\n one value.\\n* Maximum key length \u2013 128 Unicode characters in UTF-8\\n* Maximum value length \u2013 256 Unicode characters in UTF-8\\n* Allowed characters\\n\\n + Although EC2 allows for any character in its tags, other AWS services are more restrictive.\\n The allowed characters across all AWS services are: letters (`a-z`,\\n `A-Z`), numbers (`0-9`), and spaces\\n representable in UTF-8, and the following characters: `+ - = . _ :\\n / @`.\\n + If you enable instance tags in instance metadata, instance tag *keys* can only use letters (`a-z`,\\n `A-Z`), numbers (`0-9`), and the following\\n characters: `+ - = . , _ : @`. Instance tag *keys* can't contain spaces or\\n `/`, and can't comprise only `.` (one period),\\n `..` (two periods), or `_index`. For more\\n information, see View tags for your EC2 instances using instance metadata.\\n* Tag keys and values are case-sensitive.\\n* The `aws:` prefix is reserved for AWS use. If a tag has a tag key\\n with this prefix, then you can't edit or delete the tag's key or value. Tags\\n with the `aws:` prefix do not count against your tags per resource\\n limit.\\n\\nYou can't terminate, stop, or delete a resource based solely on its tags; you must specify\\nthe resource identifier. For example, to delete snapshots that you tagged with a tag key\\ncalled `DeleteMe`, you must use the `DeleteSnapshots` action with\\nthe resource identifiers of the snapshots, such as `snap-1234567890abcdef0`.\\n\\nWhen you tag public or shared resources, the tags you assign are available only to\\nyour AWS account; no other AWS account will have access to those tags. For tag-based\\naccess control to shared resources, each AWS account must assign its own set of tags to\\ncontrol access to the resource. For an exception to this rule, see Sharing tags\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/Using_Tags.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"New Amazon EC2 Feature: Resource Tagging | AWS News Blog\",\"context\":\"## AWS News Blog\\n\\n# New Amazon EC2 Feature: Resource Tagging\\n\\n It is really easy to start up that first Amazon EC2 instance, and then another, and another as you find more and more ways to put it to use. It is really easy to create some EBS volumes, attach them to your instances, and to store lots and lots of data on them. The same goes for other EC2 resources such as security groups, and EBS snapshots.\\n\\nAs your usage starts to grow from one instance and one application to many instances spanning multiple applications, it can be difficult to track which instances are assigned to which application, which EBS volumes store what data, and so forth.\\n\\nWe\u2019ve just released a very powerful **tagging** feature to allow you to tag your EC2 resources (and also certain shared resources) using up to ten key-value pairs per resource. Each tag consists of a key (up to 128 characters) and a value (up to 256 characters). The tags are stored in the AWS cloud as part of your AWS account, and are private to the account.\\n\\nYou can tag the following types of resources: EC2 instances, Amazon Machine Images (AMIs), EBS volumes, EBS snapshots, and Amazon VPC resources such as VPCs, subnets, connections, and gateways. You can tag existing resources and you can tag new resources right after you create them.\\n\\nYou can manipulate your tags using three new API calls:\\n\\n> **CreateTags** allows you to tag one or more EC2 resources with one or more tags.\\n>\\n> **DescribeTags** gives you the tags associated with one or more resources. The returned tags can be filtered by resource identifier, resource type, key, or value. You can, for example, retrieve all of the tags for a given resource, or you can retrieve all of the resources (regardless of type) with a given tag.\\n>\\n> **DeleteTags** allows you to delete a set of tags from a set of resources.\\n\\nThe existing EC2 \u201cDescribe\u201d APIs (**DescribeInstances**, **DescribeVolumes**, and so forth) return the tags associated with each of the resources in the response.\\n\\nYou can also manipulate them using the EC2 command-line tools (**ec2-create-tags**, **ec2-describe-tags**, and **ec2-delete-tags**) and from the AWS Management Console.\\n\\nYou can create and delete tags using the AWS Management Console. You can view the tags associated\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-amazon-ec2-feature-resource-tagging/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Now Organize Your AWS Resources by Using up to 50 Tags per Resource | AWS Security Blog\",\"context\":\"## AWS Security Blog\\n\\n# Now Organize Your AWS Resources by Using up to 50 Tags per Resource\\n\\n**Note:** On December 28, 2017, we updated the table and downloadable documents in this blog post.\\n\\n---\\n\\nTagging AWS resources simplifies the way you organize and discover resources, allocate costs, and control resource access across services. Many of you have told us that as the number of applications, teams, and projects running on AWS increases, you need more than 10 tags per resource. Based on this feedback, we now support up to 50 tags per resource. You do not need to take additional action\u2014you can begin applying as many as 50 tags per resource today.\\n\\nWith tags, you can use resource groups to filter resources across services and create dashboards to help you manage resources. Tag Editor enables you to tag one or more resources at a time in the AWS Management Console. To help you categorize, track, and explore your AWS costs, you can use Cost Explorer and cost allocation tags to obtain detailed billing reports. Additionally, some AWS services enable you to control access to resources based on tags by using IAM policies.\\n\\nAs of September 29, 2016, the following services and their corresponding resource types support 50 tags. (You can also download the complete list as a Word document or text file.)\\n\\nIf you have comments about this post, submit them in the \u201cComments\u201d section below.\\n\\n\u2013 Durgesh\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/now-organize-your-aws-resources-by-using-up-to-50-tags-per-resource/\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Checking AWS documentation for EC2 tag limits per instance."}

{"id": "a5c56007-a082-480d-85c3-a9eb1dd89471", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "You can attach up to **50 tags** per EC2 instance (or any AWS resource, generally). A few key restrictions to keep in mind:

- Each tag key must be unique per resource, with only one value per key
- Max key length: 128 Unicode characters
- Max value length: 256 Unicode characters
- Tags with the `aws:` prefix are reserved for AWS use and don't count against your 50-tag limit

Let me know if you want help checking tags on any of your actual instances.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
